newsitem.title: KENYA: U.N. environment body adopts U.S.-backed reform.
newsitem.headline: U.N. environment body adopts U.S.-backed reform.

text.p: The U.N. environment agency has adopted a U.S.-backed proposal for its operations to be overseen by a senior committee as part of reforms to the U.N. system.

The U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) said its governing council after two days of debate in Nairobi agreed on Friday to create a high-level committee of ministers and officials in charge of environment.
"The new committee will have the mandate to consider the international environmental agenda and to make reform and policy recommendations to the governing council," a UNEP statement said on Saturday.
It said the committee was also empowered to give "guidance and advice" to UNEP's executive director, a Canadian, to enhance cooperation with other bodies and mobilise financial resources.

"This is a great step forwards for the environment," said UNEP Executive Director Elizabeth Dowdeswell. "UNEP is now better equipped and empowered to evolve into the strong global environment organisation that the world desperately needs."
The committee will consist of 36 elected members, serving for two years, and will meet in Nairobi at least once a year.
The decision on Friday formally ended a governing council session which broke up in disarray in February with the United States, Britain and Spain threatening to withhold 1997 budget contributions.
The decisive issue was the U.S-backed proposal for the creation of the high-level committee to oversee the agency.
It had been an acrimonious and inconclusive start at the only global agency based in the Third World to the campaign for wholesale reform of the U.N. system pledged by Secretary-General Kofi Annan.

In a compromise apparently to blunt opposition to the new committee from some permanent representatives of its 185 member states, the governing council on Friday also decided to strengthen the Committee of Permanent Representatives (CPR).

The committee of Nairobi-based diplomats, some of whom argued in February that the U.S.-backed committee proposal would effectively reduce their role to "postmen", will hold now four meetings a year and was given a revised, wider mandate.
Its mandate includes reviewing implementation of governing council decisions on administrative, budgetary and programme matters and reviewing UNEP's draft work and budget programme.
The CPR was also given authority to review reports on the effectiveness, efficiency and transparency of the secretariat.
The governing council meeting in February ironically agreed to strengthen UNEP's role and approved a budget for 1998/99 of $107.5 million, arresting an erosion of UNEP funding during the 1990s.
